subject: Civil Engineering
title: Weirs and Flumes: Measuring Flow
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Weirs and Flumes: Measuring Flow.

hook.text: How much water flows in a stream? Put a barrier across it and measure the overflow.

buildup.text: A weir is a low dam with a notch. Water depth over the crest reveals the flow rate.

discovery.text: V-notch weirs measure low flows precisely. Rectangular weirs handle larger flows.

twist.text: Parshall flumes narrow the channel instead — no dam needed, less sediment buildup.

climax.text: Every irrigation district and water treatment plant uses weirs or flumes for flow measurement.

punchline.text: You can't manage water you can't measure. Weirs make invisible flow visible.

quiz.question: How does a weir measure water flow rate?
options: It measures the speed of water using sensors in the channel
Water depth over the weir crest is converted to flow rate using a formula
It counts the number of waves passing per minute

details.summary: Weirs and flumes are hydraulic structures that measure open channel flow by creating a known relationship between water depth and discharge. Weirs obstruct flow over a shaped crest while flumes constrict flow through a narrowed channel section.
details.whyItMatters: Accurate flow measurement is essential for water resource allocation, treatment plant operation, flood monitoring, and regulatory compliance. Weirs and flumes provide reliable measurement without complex electronic equipment.
takeaways: V-notch weirs accurately measure low flows while rectangular weirs handle larger discharges
Parshall flumes measure flow through channel constriction without damming the stream
Flow rate is calculated from upstream depth using calibrated rating equations for each structure

faq.question: How does a weir convert a depth measurement into a flow rate?
faq.answer: Water flowing over a weir crest accelerates to critical flow velocity, creating a unique relationship between upstream depth and discharge. Standard weir equations derived from fluid mechanics relate flow rate to the head above the crest raised to a power.

faq.question: When is a flume preferred over a weir for flow measurement?
faq.answer: Flumes are preferred when head loss must be minimized because they do not dam the channel. They handle sediment-laden flows better because velocity through the constriction keeps material moving. They work well in flat channels where a weir would cause excessive upstream flooding.
